stories.headline: Yankees don't expect Aaron Judge (calf) back for wild card
stories.summary: Aaron Judge is not expected to be available for the Yankees' wild-card series as he continues to recover from a calf strain.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- Yankees manager Aaron Boone said he does not expect to have Aaron Judge available for the Wild Card series next week, though he did not completely rule out the star right fielder recovering from his calf strain in time to play.

"We're planning on him not being a part of that," Boone said Tuesday before the Yankees hosted the Tampa Bay Rays for a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.

Judge was placed on the injured list with a right calf strain Friday, two days after exiting a game against the Minnesota Twins with the injury. Judge and the team declined to specify the severity of the injury through the weekend. On Tuesday, Boone labeled it a "moderate grade" strain. He said Judge received a PPP injection Monday and will avoid physical activity over the "next couple days."

"You hear all the time with injuries, we get ranges," Boone said. "Two to four weeks, four to six, all these things. There are ranges for a reason, and we're at a point in the year where obviously we push it a little bit if that was in play. But that's a week away so I'm not expecting it, but I'm not ruling it out either."

Judge, 34, sustained the injury in his seventh game back after missing more than three months with a fractured rib. The three-time MVP returned without going on a rehab assignment and went 4-for-23 with 13 strikeouts, one walk, and one home run in 24 plate appearances. He will likely finish his injury-plagued campaign with a .241 batting average, 18 home runs and an .871 OPS in just 66 games after two historic MVP seasons.

Heliot Ramos will start in right field for the fourth straight game since Judge's absence in Tuesday's opener. Spencer Jones is another option to play right field in the postseason should Trent Grisham, who is on the injured list with a hamstring injury, return to play center field.

The Rays entered Tuesday's doubleheader with a magic number of one to clinch the American League East title with seven games remaining. Barring a Rays collapse, the Yankees will host the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card series for the second consecutive year.

stories.body:
Feyenoord right back Givairo Read has caught the eye of Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City, while Manchester United are monitoring Borussia Dortmund striker Serhou Guirassy and Vålerenga's 15-year-old winger Gabriel Rajkovic. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Liverpool are monitoring Feyenoord right back Givairo Read but face competition from Arsenal and Manchester City, according to TEAMtalk. The 20-year-old Netherlands U21 international has registered four assists in seven Eredivisie appearances this season, with all three clubs continuing to track his progress following summer interest. A January move remains an option depending on formal approaches, after Nottingham Forest and AS Roma previously submitted offers of around €20 million that came to nothing.

- Manchester United are monitoring Borussia Dortmund striker Serhou Guirassy as they assess attacking options ahead of January, TEAMtalk reports. The 30-year-old is being considered as an experienced option should Joshua Zirkzee depart, while United remain committed to Benjamin Šeško despite his recent injury issues. Dortmund are reluctant to let Guirassy leave, but his contract has less than two years remaining, which could force their hand. Meanwhile, The Sun reports that United are targeting Vålerenga's 15-year-old winger Gabriel Rajkovic as a replacement for JJ Gabriel.

Barca's head of scouting, João Amaral, reportedly watched the 19-year-old against Bahia, with Tottenham Hotspur, Newcastle United and Atlético Madrid also among his admirers. The left-footed defender, who earned a call-up to Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil squad, has a transfer value of around €30 million and after Spurs previously had a €21 million offer for 80% of his economic rights rejected.

The 33-year-old striker has been available since leaving Galatasaray in July, but Spurs are wary of his wage demands and lack of Premier League experience. Serie A is considered the likeliest destination for the former Sampdoria, Inter Milan and PSG star, with Lazio among several interested Italian clubs.

stories.headline: WNBA Power Rankings: What went right for every team this season
stories.summary: What's the best thing that happened for every WNBA team this season? We break it down.
stories.body:
We're at the end of the line for ESPN's weekly WNBA Power Rankings. The regular season concludes Thursday. The playoffs begin Sunday for eight teams, and the other seven look toward the offseason. And for the Connecticut Sun, there is a move south to Houston and name change to the Comets.

It's an exciting finish because playoff seeding is still not wrapped up. While that plays out, in these last Power Rankings we will look at the best thing that happened this season for each team.

Every franchise had some positive developments, some of which could be building blocks for 2027.

1. Golden State Valkyries (31-11)
Previous ranking: 1

Rest of the regular season: @ POR (Sept. 22), @ LA (Sept. 24)

The Valkyries' addition of versatile forward Gabby Williams in free agency was a key part of their improvement from the No. 8 seed in their 2025 inaugural season to a No. 1 or 2 seed this year. Williams, whose defensive prowess goes back to her days at UConn, was the perfect fit for the WNBA's top defense in 2026. She also leads Golden State in scoring (14.3 PPG). The Valkyries beat Portland 82-66 and Seattle 70-57 last week to cross the 30-win threshold and secure home-court advantage in the first round.

2. Minnesota Lynx (32-10)
Previous ranking: 2

Rest of the regular season: @ IND (Sept. 22), vs. IND (Sept. 24)

Last year, the Lynx needed a point guard, and they got a great one with No. 2 pick Olivia Miles. She clicked with coach Cheryl Reeve, who trusted Miles to quarterback the offense, and Miles is now a lock for the Rookie of the Year award, averaging team highs of 19.8 points and 6.0 assists. But despite owning the league's best record going into their last two games, the Lynx haven't been as sharp as hoped while closing out the season. They lost their two games before the FIBA World Cup break, then their first game after it: 93-81 to New York at home Friday. Minnesota then pounded Connecticut 101-89 Sunday but will finish with back-to-back games against Indiana, which is fighting for a better playoff seed.

3. Las Vegas Aces (29-13)
Previous ranking: 3

Rest of the regular season: vs. LA (Sept. 22), @ PHO (Sept. 24)

The best part of 2026 for the Aces has been that their big three -- A'ja Wilson, Jackie Young and Chelsea Gray -- is still going strong in its sixth season together. In today's pro sports world, how often does a trio of stars get that much time as a unit? The defending champion Aces haven't had the extreme highs and lows of last year's regular season, but they will end up with a similar record and momentum heading into the playoffs. Wilson and Young combined for 117 points, 19 rebounds and 22 assists in two blowout wins over Seattle this past week, 114-77 Thursday and 98-77 Sunday, and Wilson appears on her way to her fifth MVP award.

4. Atlanta Dream (29-14)
Previous ranking: 5

Rest of the regular season: @ NY (Sept. 23)

The Dream's offense is on fire. This past week, Atlanta beat Connecticut 103-59, Chicago 106-81 and New York 95-84, moving closer to securing a top-four playoff seed. The best thing that happened for this team -- and a big reason for that success -- was obtaining Angel Reese in a trade with Chicago. The Dream have relied heavily on Reese to replace two of their top rebounders from last season: Brionna Jones, who was limited to nine games by leg injuries, and Brittney Griner, who signed with Connecticut. Reese is leading the WNBA in rebounding average (12.3 per game) for the third season in a row.

5. New York Liberty (26-17)
Previous ranking: 6

Rest of the regular season: vs. ATL (Sept. 23)

The Liberty got a confidence boost with a 93-81 win at Minnesota on Friday, then followed that with a 106-69 blowout of Toronto on Sunday. But Monday's 95-84 loss at home to Atlanta ended the Liberty's chances of being a top-four seed. With prized free agent Satou Sabally limited to 13 games because of concussion issues, this hasn't been the season the Liberty were hoping for -- although it still could be with a strong playoff run. But one bright spot was the emergence of French rookie guard Pauline Astier, who has started 38 games and averaged 9.4 points and 3.4 assists.

6. Washington Mystics (26-16)
Previous ranking: 8

Rest of the regular season: vs. CON (Sept. 22), vs. CHI (Sept. 24)

Being the WNBA's youngest team has been no impediment for the Mystics, who are back in the playoffs after a two-year absence. The highlight has been the play of center Shakira Austin, the No. 3 draft pick in 2022, who fully realized her potential this season. She is averaging career highs in points (17.2), rebounds (9.4) and assists (2.6). The Mystics returned from the World Cup break with two road victories: 110-80 at Chicago on Thursday and 93-77 at Indiana on Sunday. Washington has gone 14-4 since July 20 and has become a team to watch in the playoffs.

7. Indiana Fever (27-15)
Previous ranking: 6

Rest of the regular season: vs. MIN (Sept. 22), @ MIN (Sept. 24)

Having a healthy Caitlin Clark back after she was limited by injuries to 13 games in 2025 has been the best part of the season for Indiana. Not just for all she does and the excitement she brings but how well the backcourt of Clark (22.7 PPG, 8.4 APG) and Kelsey Mitchell (25.1 PPG) plays together. They've been the engine powering the Fever all season, with Indiana hitting the 100-point mark a record 20 times. But when the offense is off, Indiana is in trouble, and such was the case Sunday in a 93-77 loss to Washington. Now the Fever finish their season with two games against the Lynx, still fighting for seeding.

8. Dallas Wings (26-17)
Previous ranking: 7

Rest of the regular season: @ SEA (Sept. 23)

With victories this past week against Los Angeles (97-77) and Phoenix (87-82), the Wings had won six in a row. But on Monday, they let a 14-point lead slip away in an 87-86 loss at Phoenix. Still, Dallas is headed back to the playoffs after a two-year absence. While everyone expected another great year from Paige Bueckers, Jessica Shepard has been a game changer in her first season with the Wings. A candidate for most improved player, she is averaging 14.3 points, 11.1 rebounds and 5.1 assists.

9. Los Angeles Sparks (16-26)
Previous ranking: 10

Rest of the regular season: @ LV (Sept. 22), vs. GS (Sept. 24)

It's a sad end to the season for L.A., as Nneka Ogwumike will retire and the Sparks will miss the playoffs for the sixth year in a row. Ogwumike is finishing a Hall of Fame career on a high note, as she led the Sparks in scoring, rebounding and assists in their two games last week: a 97-77 loss at Dallas and a 105-84 win over Portland. The season's biggest positive was the development of younger players such as Rae Burrell, who will be a restricted free agent in 2027, and Cameron Brink, who will be on the last year of her rookie contract in 2027. Both could be an important part of the Sparks' next chapter; a new general manager, Ariana Andonian, will try to get the three-time champion franchise back on track.

10. Phoenix Mercury (16-27)
Previous ranking: 11

Rest of the regular season: vs. LV (Sept. 24)

The Mercury, who made the WNBA Finals last season, won't be going to the playoffs -- but they are still battling until the end. After beating Portland 94-91 on Thursday, they fell at Dallas 87-82 on Saturday. But then Phoenix won 87-86 in the rematch with the Wings on Monday at home, led by Kahleah Copper's 31 points. She has been the best part of a disappointing season for Phoenix, as she averaged a career-high 21.6 points.

11. Portland Fire (16-27)
Previous ranking: 9

Rest of the regular season: vs. GS (Sept. 22)

Golden State making the playoffs in its first season last year was the exception. The rule is that expansion teams must get their feet under them before they can compete for the postseason. Based on that timeline, Portland has had a promising first season, though the end hasn't been as strong. The Fire fell in their three games this past week -- to Phoenix (94-91), Golden State (82-66) and Los Angeles (105-84) -- and have lost seven of their past eight. The brightest spot for Portland this season was French guard Carla Leite, its second pick in the expansion draft. Just 22 and in her second WNBA season, Leite led the Fire in scoring (16.0 per game) and assists (6.3).

12. Chicago Sky (15-27)
Previous ranking: 12

Rest of the regular season: vs. TOR (Sept. 22), @ WAS (Sept. 24)

The Sky, who lost 110-80 to Washington and 106-81 to Atlanta last week, will miss the playoffs for the third year in a row and remain a franchise looking for its identity. Before the season, Chicago traded Angel Reese to Atlanta, a move that didn't sit well with many of the team's fans. The Sky also obtained Rickea Jackson in a trade with Los Angeles, but she played just four games before an ACL injury ended her season. One of their big free agent signings, Skylar Diggins, was limited to 19 games by injury. One of the gold nuggets of the season was signing guard Sydney Taylor, who went undrafted in 2024 when her college career ended. She has averaged 13.4 points as a rookie and hit some big shots in Sky victories.

13. Connecticut Sun (10-32)
Previous ranking: 13

Rest of the regular season: @ WAS (Sept. 22), vs. TOR (Sept. 24)

The Sun will end their chapter in the WNBA on Thursday. League followers should not forget how important the Mohegan Tribe's stewardship was when it became the league's first independent owners in 2003, taking over the short-lived Orlando Miracle. It kept the league from losing that franchise altogether, which is what happened five years later to the Houston Comets. Next year, the Sun will leave Uncasville, Connecticut -- a small town the WNBA outgrew -- for Houston and revive the Comets. Last week, Connecticut fell 103-59 at Atlanta and 101-89 at home to Minnesota. Despite those blowouts, the best part of 2026 for the Sun was that they didn't just mail in the season. They still reached double-digit victories and will not finish last. They say goodbye to the Mohegan Sun Arena on Thursday, and we'll watch to see what this franchise looks like next year.

14. Seattle Storm (8-35)
Previous ranking: 14

Rest of the regular season: vs. DAL (Sept. 23)

The Storm knew this season would be about developing young players under a new coaching system. Seattle, which lost twice last week, will finish with the league's worst record but ahead of Toronto for the second-to-last spot in the Power Rankings thanks to a small edge: The Storm have won three games since the start of July to the Tempo's two. The promise of the future is the best part of Seattle's 2026: centers Dominique Malonga and Awa Fam are both 20, and guard Flau'jae Johnson is 22. They combined to average 43.5% of the Storm's scoring this season.

15. Toronto Tempo (11-31)
Previous ranking: 15

Rest of the season: @ CHI (Sept. 22), @ CON (Sept. 24)

Toronto lost 103-85 to Indiana and 106-69 to New York last week. But the Tempo's 2026 highlight had nothing to do with their record: They made history this season as the first WNBA team outside the United States. Toronto also had a dynamic guard trio -- when those guards were healthy. Marina Mabrey was limited to 32 games and Brittney Sykes 17; they are shut down for the season. Rookie Kiki Rice has played 26 games, scoring in double figures in the past 11. Having all three at full strength and upgrading post play could make 2027 a better season for the Tempo.

stories.body:
"The Hoop Collective" podcast, hosted by ESPN's Brian Windhorst, releases episodes every Monday, Wednesday and Friday during the NBA season and Tuesday and Friday during the offseason. Windhorst and his guests break down what's happening on and off the court, evaluating the trends you need to know and examining the latest news from across the NBA.

There's never been a guy in that kind of a situation who signed for the qualifying offer. The closest comp you can get to that is actually another Pistons big man. It was Greg Monroe, but it was completely different circumstances."

Windhorst on a potential Brandon Miller extension in Charlotte: "I think if it's a five-year deal, I think you're looking for that. Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to cover the latest fallout from the LA Clippers' punishment after the NBA announced its punishments for the franchise's off-the-court dealings with Kawhi Leonard. They discuss what league history could tell us about what's ahead for the Clippers and how LA got into this situation. They then close on key deals in the West, including Ben Simmons signing with the Sacramento Kings and Amen Thompson's extension with the Houston Rockets.

Topics:

0:27: Updates on the fallout from Clippers' punishment

Windhorst on the league's reaction to the Clippers' punishment: "I think Steve Balmer had support of his peers in this, even though these was pretty severe accusations.

"I'm not saying everybody again, but I think people wanted to believe him, his peers. I'm not talking about the other GMs. I'm not talking about the agents. ...

"So the word that was said to me by a very influential person was that the other owners, some of the other owners were aghast when they read this report. That was the word that was used to me, aghast. And regardless of what Steve says, the support that he had is no longer there."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action now: "When the Wolves were found guilty, Glen Taylor said words that were not, "I'm guilty." Kevin McHale, who was the vice president of basketball operations, said, 'I didn't even know this existed.' You know, he pled ignorance.

"[Then] They thought about it. They ended up negotiating with the league office and they pled guilty. And two days after basically they raised the white flag in December, David Stern gave him back a pick and a year later he gave him back the second pick. Now he gave them back -- he took away five years of picks [previously] -- he gave them back Year 3 at first and then Year 5. It wasn't like he gave him back immediately. But I think the Clippers should study that."

MacMahon on why Houston extended Thompson now: "I've been telling you for a while just how much the Rockets value Thompson. If there's one untradeable player on the roster, it is him.

"According to their metrics, they think he's one of the top 10 -- and I might be inflating that number -- most valuable players in the league. Now, we can argue and we can debate and you can say that's ridiculous. I'm just telling you the way that they view him. And so for them to get a player they value that much on this deal is great value for them.

"And for Amen Thompson, $208 million fully guaranteed and there's no options either way in the deal, he's set for life. He wants to be in Houston. He's going to be in Houston."

stories.headline: Predictions for every NHL team in 2026-27: Playoffs, milestones, more
stories.summary: We're not saying all of these will come true ... but a lot of them just might!
stories.body:
With the 2026-27 NHL season nearly here, it's time to make some bold predictions about what will and will not happen on the way to handing out the Stanley Cup.

Last season, I went 14-18 in these predictions and was quite close to breaking even. Let's see how many of these bold predictions for the NHL's 32 teams come to pass.

These educated guesses range from statistical achievements to awards predictions to coach firings to Stanley Cup playoffs prognostications. Enjoy, and welcome back, hockey!

How to watch the 2026-27 NHL season on ESPN networks -- including 100 exclusive games and the out-of-market package (over 1,050 games).

Atlantic Division

Boston Bruins
Pavel Zacha regresses

Despite rampant trade rumors involving center-desperate teams taking a long look at a $4.75 million cap hit, the Bruins have held onto Zacha. Last season, that decision was rewarded with a 30-goal season, to go along with his usual defensive reliability.

Boston has several scoring forwards who could be primed for regression this season, but chief among them is Zacha. He had a 22.9% shooting percentage last season, which is higher than that of Morgan Geekie (21.5%), their 39-goal scoring winger. It's also the first time Zacha's shooting percentage was higher than 16.5% in his career.

As Geekie proved last season, just because a player's shooting percentage has an elephantine increase year-over-year doesn't guarantee regression -- Geekie shot 22% and scored 33 goals two years ago. But Zacha isn't playing with David Pastrnak. He played a bunch with Casey Mittelstadt last season, a player who might also be in line for a statistical decline.

Buffalo Sabres
Jarmo swings a deadline blockbuster

Jarmo Kekalainen was officially hired as the Sabres' GM on Dec. 15. They went 36-9-5 after that, breaking the NHL's longest postseason drought while winning a playoff round before losing to the Montreal Canadiens in seven games.

What will Buffalo do for an encore? I wouldn't punch their ticket for a second straight trip to the playoffs just yet, if only because that 109-point season is going to be tough to replicate with a resurgent Panthers team, a healthier Lightning club and an improving group of Canadiens. But the Sabres have shown enough to earn Kekalainen's confidence that they're building something special in Buffalo -- and when a team earns Kekalainen's confidence, that's usually when he takes his biggest swings.

Recall that he made aggressive trades for Marian Gaborik, Seth Jones, Brandon Saad, Scott Hartnell, Artemi Panarin and Matt Duchene while managing the Blue Jackets. I think he makes that kind of move to level up the Sabres this season. Maybe it's finding the right deal to pry Connor Hellebuyck from the Jets' stubborn hands, a player they've reportedly been pursuing. Maybe it's a center who is healthier than Josh Norris. Whatever the target, Kekalainen takes his shot before the deadline.

Detroit Red Wings
Dylan Larkin stays in Detroit

The Red Wings' now former captain wasn't exactly forthcoming in his first meeting with reporters since his trade request became public. In particular, Larkin didn't explain whether his ill feelings toward the organization stemmed from his dealings with general manager Steve Yzerman and whether Yzerman's departure from that role this summer might have mended any of those fences with the organization.

He also wouldn't go into details about his list of preferred destinations, and therein lies the rub for the Red Wings and Larkin: Unless either his list gets larger or their expected return for him grows smaller, he's going to be skating for Detroit. (Sorry, Minnesota Wild.)

So the prediction here is that both sides grit their teeth, honor his contract and have Larkin play the full season in Detroit. There will be boos from fans and uncomfortable questions from reporters, at least at the start. But as the games go on, one thing remains clear: The Red Wings are a better team with Larkin in the middle than without him, and they know that.

Florida Panthers
Win the Stanley Cup

What, did you think the Cats' dynasty had crumbled? Did you think this brief respite from their consecutive runs to the Stanley Cup Final -- a breather for the rest of the NHL, brought to you by the tendons in Aleksander Barkov's knee -- was proof that their contention window was closed?

If you're sick of the Panthers, both as champions and the sport's leading trolls, here's the unfortunate news:

They're going to win the Stanley Cup again, their third chalice in four seasons.

Some conditions have changed since the last time the Panthers were victorious, and those changes do give me pause:

Sergei Bobrovsky is in Toronto, and they're replaced him with the wildly inconsistent Jacob Markstrom.
Evan Rodrigues, an essential ingredient in their special sauce, was traded to the Devils for Markstrom.
Perhaps most importantly, the NHL and the NHLPA agreed to a postseason salary cap and long-term injured reserve rules that were instituted last season. We've already seen what that can do to Florida, which was unable to replace Barkov's salary when he went down in the preseason, lest the Panthers lose the chance to bring him back for the playoffs.

Of course, they didn't make the playoffs, which means they got extra recovery time after having played more hockey in the previous three seasons than any other team. The foundation of those Cup runs remains in intact: No one in the NHL can match their top three lines and top two defense pairings, especially with the addition of Brady Tkachuk.

(Scoff at Tkachuk's playoff pedigree if you want, but he's going to be in the same situation Mitch Marner was last season for Vegas, entering a ring-filled locker room as one of many instead of "the man." Look how that turned out.)

The only question is whether that talent up front can outkick its downgrade in goal, and I assume it will -- or that GM Bill Zito, one of the best in the business, will creatively upgrade that position if necessary.

Fans start lining up under the balcony at the Elbo Room now for beer showers from the Stanley Cup again.

Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson, Norris Finalist

Sometimes, offensive defensemen win the Norris Trophy because their offensive accomplishments are just that overwhelming. Think Quinn Hughes popping for 92 points when he won in 2024, or Erik Karlsson winning his first Norris in 2012 with 78 points in 81 games.

Hutson had that kind of season in 2025-26 with 78 points in 82 games, skating to a plus-36. Yet he finished sixth in voting for the Norris. Evan Bouchard of the Oilers had an even more bonkers offensive season, with 95 points in 82 games, but he finished fourth. Which brings us to another tenet of the Norris Trophy: Sometimes elite offensive defensemen need to convince the voters, rightly or wrongly, that they're not one-dimensional players.

I think Hutson did that during the Habs' run to the Eastern Conference finals last season. It was an eye-opening performance, with defensive defenseman royalty Jaccob Slavin comparing Hutson's game to that of Hughes during Carolina's series against Montreal. Those kinds of endorsements go a long way toward eventually making a Norris case for Hutson.

Assuming the Canadiens are a playoff team again, it might be "his turn" to make the Norris top three. (It being a player's "turn" is another hallmark of the Norris, as Zach Werenski and Rasmus Dahlin witnessed last season.)

Ottawa Senators
Miss the playoffs

The Senators aren't going to suddenly fall apart without Brady Tkachuk. In fact, there are some reasons to believe they're going to be better positioned to succeed this season, especially if they get goaltending worthy of their excellent even-strength defense (second overall in expected goals against per 60 minutes last season).

That said, Tkachuk was still a point-per-game player for the Senators. Due respect to William Eklund, a solid pickup from the Sharks in June, but he's not going to able to replicate that output.

Ottawa was a 99-point team last season. I think the Sens probably fall between five to eight points from that pace and miss the playoffs, before what could be a big bounce-back in 2027-28.

Tampa Bay Lightning
Nikita Kucherov signs a new deal for less than $20M AAV

Kucherov gave fans the quote of the preseason when he was asked how the game had changed during his career: "The game is faster, but very dumb. Low IQ." Incredible.

Also very dumb: Anyone concerned that Kucherov might not end up signing another contract with the Lightning, with unrestricted free agency looming after this season. The 33-year-old superstar winger has everything he needs in Tampa: lovely weather, talented teammates on an annually contending team, and the complete lack of pressure to be anything other than what he is when it comes to public or media relations responsibilities. He just gets to be Kuch and score 100-plus points. Why would he ever leave that?

It has been reported that Kucherov might be seeking a $20 million AAV on this contract. It's hard to imagine that not being reported for every star player whose deal is up in a post-Cale Makar contract landscape. Given the Lightning's incredible cap situation -- they have Brayden Point ($9.5 million), Jake Guentzel ($9 million) and Brandon Hagel ($6.5 million) all locked in under $10 million annually through 2030 -- Kucherov could ask for that AAV without annihilating their financial structure.

But I think, ultimately, Kucherov comes in under $20 million annually. He'll swap that for term, potentially for six seasons, and the security that he'll probably finish his career as a Bolt.

He'll make more than countryman Kirill Kaprizov ($17 million AAV) but less than the $20 million mark. Which no doubt will spark another round of "state income tax advantages" conjecture regarding a Florida team.

Toronto Maple Leafs
Miss the playoffs again

Some teams make changes. The Toronto Maple Leafs made, like, all the changes. New management, new coaches, almost a dozen new players on the roster, from the top UFA defenseman (Darren Raddysh) to the top pick in the NHL draft(Gavin McKenna).

While there was certainly a "let's throw everything at the wall and see what sticks" vibe to GM John Chayka's offseason spree, that doesn't mean it can't work. While building chemistry is paramount, the health of the roster will make or break the season. That starts with Auston Matthews, coming off knee surgery and having not played since March 12. It certainly includes Chris Tanev, the veteran defensive defenseman who was limited to just 11 games last season.

The Leafs would need somewhere around a 20-point improvement to make the Stanley Cup playoffs again, after missing for the first time in 10 seasons. It's not an unreasonable target, but I'm not convinced they hit it.

I'm worried about the fragility of some of the bodies on the roster, including that of Anthony Stolarz, who will be tasked with being the safety net for Sergei Bobrovsky's regular season decline. I'm concerned about how the pieces fit behind what should be two terrific forward lines with Matthews and John Tavares as center. While I'm interested in coach Jim Hiller getting a chance to flex his offensive acumen after he said he was forced to play a more defensive scheme with the Los Angeles Kings roster he was dealt, I'm not sold on him as a head coach.

They'll be better, but not good enough.

Metropolitan Division

Carolina Hurricanes
Jordan Staal wins the Selke Trophy

This shouldn't be a bold prediction. Staal should be on his third Selke by now. Unfortunately, he has played in an era that saw the award dominated by Patrice Bergeron, Aleksander Barkov, Anze Kopitar and Pavel Datsyuk.

Staal just kept putting together masterful defensive seasons in Raleigh, never getting the recognition he deserved apart from a second-place finish for the Selke in 2024.

Well, he got recognition last postseason: Staal won the Conn Smythe as playoff MVP as the Hurricanes won the Stanley Cup. He deserved it as a defensive force, but it was his six goals in the Final series against Vegas that clinched it -- an ironic accomplishment, given that his lack of offensive output in the regular season probably cost him Selke attention. (No, offensive achievement being essential for a defensive award never made sense to us, either.)

Assuming the Hurricanes are good and assuming Staal is just as good defensively as he has been season after season for them, here's predicting a "gold watch" Selke win for the captain, the byproduct of the national media lovefest he was showered with last playoffs.

Columbus Blue Jackets
Kirill Marchenko isn't traded

It's fairly obvious that Marchenko isn't long for Columbus. He was asked point-blank if that's where he wanted to be, and the 26-year-old forward would only say "I like playing hockey" while refusing to add the caveat "here" to his answer.

The rest of the league is intrigued by the idea that Marchenko, who led the Jackets in goal for three straight seasons, could be available via trade. But unless this ordeal becomes a massive distraction for the team and the fans, the Blue Jackets have no compelling reason to fulfill his desire to leave now. He's a restricted free agent next offseason. They could easily just trade him then.

For now, he's the best offensive forward for a team that was right on the playoff bubble last season.

New Jersey Devils
This is Sheldon Keefe's last season

The Devils are, as always, a team that could be at the top of the conference or back in the lottery depending on the team's overall injury situation and specifically the health of star center Jack Hughes, who has played over 70 games in a season only once in his seven-year NHL career.

There's another X factor this season: goaltending. After Jacob Markstrom proved not to be the solution to their yearslong woes, they've move on with a trio of Jake Allen, Nico Daws and David Rittich as they wait for Boston University goalie Mikhail Yegorov to potentially become that solution.

This is Keefe's third season as coach with the Devils. He's under contract for one more season beyond this one. If New Jersey underachieves during the season, or fails to make the playoffs again, that's an easy dismissal for new GM Sunny Mehta to make, given Keefe wasn't his hire. But even if the Devils make the cut and fail to advance past the first round -- they have one playoff series win since 2012 -- one could see Keefe paying for that shortfall as well.

New York Islanders
Become deadline sellers

There's only so much magic Matthew Schaefer and Ilya Sorokin can weave with this roster. Multiple projections have the Islanders under 90 points this season after a 91-point campaign that ended with coach Patrick Roy being replaced by Pete DeBoer.

That coaching change is a reason to believe the Islanders could sneak into a playoff seed, given how much immediate success DeBoer has had in his various NHL stops. But the Devils, Sharks, Golden Knights and Stars teams that all made the conference finals in his first seasons with them are much deeper than this Islanders roster.

The best case for GM Mathieu Darche and Islanders fans: That he has a good sense of where they're going to finish at the trade deadline and starts shipping out some veterans. Getting this roster closer to Schaefer's age curve than, say, Jean-Gabriel Pageau's will eventually bring the Islanders to where they want to go.

New York Rangers
Gabe Perreault doubles his goal total

The best thing to happen for this prediction was GM Chris Drury not giving Perreault the eight-year extension many assumed would come before the new NHL CBA made that contract term verboten. Drury indicated that the forward needs to continue "to grow" and "earn responsibility."

Reading between the lines of his preseason comments, as Perreault probably did, the Rangers didn't believe the 21-year-old was worth the investment yet.

What a glorious carrot to dangle in front of a player entering his second full NHL season, and one that could be in a position to thrive offensively on a line with Mika Zibanejad and Alexis Lafreniere. Most projections I've seen have him topping out at around 50 points, but with increased ice time and hopefully continued power-play success, I see him doubling his 12 goals from last season.

Philadelphia Flyers
Step back before a leap forward

There's a lot to love around the Flyers right now. They have a fantastic collection of young forwards ages 19-24 who will form the foundation of this budding contender. They have a coach in Rick Tocchet with whom they'll grow. The Flyers' goaltending, long an issue, appears solid with Dan Vladar having earned a new contract and Joseph Woll arriving from Toronto.

But when I attended Flyers camp this month, the vibe felt apprehensive. Like last season's playoff berth and elimination of the Penguins was too much, too soon, and there was a little concern about regression. I think those concerns are warranted, and Philly takes a slight step back this season while missing the playoffs. But one year of growing pains is offset by getting to watch Porter Martone lead the franchise for the next decade.

Pittsburgh Penguins
Sergei Murashov is the real deal

The Penguins made the playoffs last season thanks in part to new coach Dan Muse getting everything he could out of the supporting cast around Sidney Crosby and Evgeni Malkin. They finished second in the Metro despite having the 23rd best team save percentage in the NHL.

One thing that won't change this season is the Penguins making the playoffs, as I have them in again. One thing that will change: The effectiveness of their goaltending, thanks to Murashov. The 22-year-old rookie dominated Russian juniors, the ECHL and the AHL en route to earning a spot in the Pittsburgh crease with Arturs Silovs. He's one of the best goaltending prospects in the NHL, and there already are expectations he takes the starting job before the turn of the calendar.

Is this putting too much on a guy who was tending goal for Yaroslavl Loko Jr. two years ago? Probably. Has he earned that level of hype? He has, and based on his play and his comportment, he might meet it this season.

Washington Capitals
Make the Eastern Conference finals

The Capitals might be the one team in the Eastern Conference that can take the Florida Panthers' bludgeoning and throw it back at them.

Washington is absolutely loaded with humungous players who can skate and score: Aliaksei Protas (6-6, 250), Ilya Protas (6-6, 225), Tom Wilson (6-4, 225), Pierre-Luc Dubois (6-4, 220), Alex Tuch (6-4, 219) and a plucky ingénue named Alex Ovechkin (6-3, 238). They're going to steamroll the rest of the conference.

I love the makeup of this team, from the goaltending to their coach to the plethora of scoring options to that wonderful alchemy between veteran players and the next wave of young Capitals stars, such as Cole Hutson on defense. What I don't totally love is their back end, which is talented but lacks those Brooks Orpik/Matt Niskanen types who provided the backbone of their Stanley Cup win in 2018. Perhaps GM Chris Patrick can add a little more before the playoffs begin.

I nearly picked the Capitals to win the Stanley Cup. They have that potential, even with Ovechkin staring at the last beams of sunset in his career. Ultimately, I don't think they can match the star power and depth of the Panthers in a seven-game playoff series. But goaltender Logan Thompson could be the great equalizer.

Central Division

Chicago Blackhawks
Anton Frondell, top-three rookie scorer

This could be a good season for rookie forwards, with players such as Gavin McKenna (Maple Leafs), Porter Martone (Flyers) and Ivar Stenberg (Sharks) all looking to make an immediate impact.

Frondell, the No. 3 pick in 2025, could have the greatest impact of them all.

He had a tantalizing debut for the Blackhawks last season after coming over from Djurgardens IF of the Swedish Hockey League, with nine points in 12 games. He's going to be a force in Chicago's top six, but to really break through, he's going to need Connor Bedard back on the ice with him. Bedard is expected to sit out the first month of the season because of a shoulder injury. In the meantime, he'll have on his flank Tyler Bertuzzi, who worked well with him in their limited time together last season.

Colorado Avalanche
Win the Western Conference

The Vegas Golden Knights didn't sweep the Avalanche last season in the conference finals. They swept a broken-down shell of the Avalanche, like one of those brittle cicada exoskeletons you'd see attached to a tree trunk. Cale Makar missed two games and was limited in the other two. Nathan MacKinnon was injured. The Avs were bruised and out of sorts against a Vegas team peaking at the right time.

This is just more kindling for the fire raging inside of MacKinnon in his increasingly desperate pursuit of a second Stanley Cup win. That manifested in a career-high 53-goal season as the Avalanche finished with the league's best record in 2025-26. But the business was left unfinished in the postseason.

That motivation is one reason I like Colorado to advance in the West. Another reason: GM Joe Sakic is back in the big chair. I love the fact that he's infusing this roster with some hungry young players who will have the opportunity to play important roles. I love the fact that in his acquisition of pesky Zachary L'Heureux from Nashville, he identified a missing element on their roster: the physical, rink-rat-energy forward. I trust that Sakic isn't done refining this group.

The Avalanche haven't won a conference finals game since 2022. They'll win four of them this postseason.

Dallas Stars
Hit the John Tortorella panic button in-season

Peter DeBoer haunts the Dallas Stars. They made the conference finals in three straight seasons under DeBoer before firing him in 2025. Glen Gulutzan returned for a second stint as head coach, and the Stars lost in the first round of the playoffs to Minnesota, thanks to the current Stanley Cup Playoff format forcing the third and seventh best teams in the league to meet in the opening round.

The haunting continued in this preseason, when Gulutzan said the Stars might need "a little more 'Pete DeBoer' system in us," in reference to how the break out the puck. It was an innocent, illustrative reference ... and yet also a reminder that Gulutzan is not DeBoer in accomplishment or comportment.

The moment the Vegas Golden Knights didn't bring coach John Tortorella back after last season's run to the Stanley Cup Final, the hockey world started wondering into what coaching spot he could parachute into next. After all, Torts needed only eight regular-season games to "fix" the Knights before they won three playoff rounds.

I submit to you the Dallas Stars. They still have the players to contend for the Stanley Cup, including what might be one final season of Jason Robertson potting goals before unrestricted free agency. If the returns are diminishing under Gulutzan as the playoffs near, this could be an ideal spot for another quick-turn roster reinvigoration.

And, selfishly for content purposes, putting Tortorella on the proper side of the bracket to potentially meet the Golden Knights in the conference finals.

Minnesota Wild
Trade Jesper Wallstedt

It's hard to stuff the genie back into the bottle. Last season, Wallstedt's name was circulated as potential trade bait in Minnesota's search for the star center their lineup continues to lack. It ended up not moving him, and Wallstedt ended up having a terrific postseason as the Wild won a playoff round.

So, that's that, right? Not really. The Wild invested in goalie Filip Gustavsson with a contract that runs through 2031 and carries a $6.8 million annual cap hit. Wallstedt makes $2.2 million against the cap, but he is a restricted free agent next summer and due for a considerable raise. Combine that with his value in the trade market, and the Wall might be relocated to another room at some point, as was rumored last season.

Nashville Predators
Matthew Wood breaks out

The continuing existence of one Tage Nathaniel Thompson means that Wood probably won't be considered the best UConn alum currently playing in the NHL. But that doesn't mean he can't craft his own legacy as Huskies hockey royalty (after a one-year stint at Minnesota as well).

Wood was the No. 15 pick in the 2023 draft by Nashville, and had a nice rookie season: 17 goals and 13 assists in 71 games. Solid, but not a breakout season.

No, the breakout season happens over the next several months. Wood will earn much more than the 12:19 per game in ice time he averaged last season. He's getting a PP1 look in the preseason with Steven Stamkos, Ryan O'Reilly, Filip Forsberg and Roman Josi. He's also expected to be Forsberg's linemate at 5-on-5, having worked well with him last season.

The Predators have some offensive upside under coach Andrew Brunette, having finished 13th in expected goals scored last season at even strength. Wood is absolutely positioned to pop this season.

St. Louis Blues
Dylan Holloway goes 30/70

The Blues' offer sheet to Holloway in 2024 is already an unmitigated success. Edmonton would perform ritual sacrifice to find a 25-year-old physical winger who can pop for 26 goals on their current roster. They had one in Holloway.

He's just getting better now that he's on one of the NHL's best lines with Robert Thomas and Jimmy Snuggerud, a trio that averaged 5.7 goals per 60 minutes together last season. I think Holloway breaks the 30-goal mark and hits 70 points for the first time in his career -- although as I noted in my fantasy hockey "Plant My Flag" story this week, he's going to need an uptick in power-play production to do that.

The bold part of this prediction is that Holloway will be in the lineup enough to hit these marks, which has been a struggle in the past. But if he is, with that line cooking, it's going to be a career season.

Utah Mammoth
Trade for Connor Hellebuyck

It's no secret that Mammoth owner Ryan Smith has tried to aggressively improve his team, both in moves that the Mammoth have made and ones they've attempted to pull off. It's also no secret that Connor Hellebuyck is going to be traded somewhere by the Winnipeg Jets at some point. It's just a matter of the Jets finding the right offer to convince them to make the move.

Why Utah? Karel Vejmelka is good. Sometimes he's great. Sometimes he's not. He was 24th in goals saved above expected per 60 minutes last season (minimum 30 games), which was actually better than Hellebuyck (26th) during the multiple-Vezina Trophy winner's nightmarish season with Winnipeg. But this would be a significant upgrade in goal, and a foundation on which a young contender can be built.

The bummer here is that the Jets reportedly don't want a trade for futures, given Utah's deep pool of prospects. It also has been widely reported that the Jets want a center in return for Hellebuyck. The obvious choice is Nick Schmaltz, but he has a full no-trade clause. Barrett Hayton would have worked, but he's a UFA after this season.

Could the Jets do this for 19-year-old blue-chip prospect Caleb Desnoyers? Would Utah do that? I don't know. I think the biggest issue might be Winnipeg trading Hellebuyck within its own division. But the bold prediction is the bold prediction for a reason.

Winnipeg Jets
Scott Arniel is fired

While a 34-point decline in the standings was severe for the Jets last season, it should be noted that drop started from the 116 points they amassed in winning the Presidents' Trophy in coach Scott Arniel's first season. But there were real causes for concern for Winnipeg last season beyond missing the playoffs, as they saw a small decline in expected goals scored and a steeper one in expected goals against at 5-on-5. As mediocre (by his standards) Connor Hellebuyck was last season, the defense front of him was 19th in the league in that metric.

GM Kevin Cheveldayoff danced around Arniel's status after last season, saying "we're not ready to turn the page on anything yet." But if Winnipeg gets off to another bum start -- and the Hellebuyck situation isn't helping -- dismissing a coach in the last year of his contract would seem like a typical desperation move.

Pacific Division

Anaheim Ducks
Take a step back

Leo Carlsson's offer sheet with the Flyers, and Cutter Gauthier's subsequent contract drama, overshadowed what was an underwhelming offseason for a burgeoning contender that won a playoff round last postseason.

With the departures of Jacob Trouba, Radko Gudas and trade deadline pickup John Carlson, the defense corps doesn't have a player over the age of 25 on it to start the season. Giving players such as Ian Moore, Tristan Luneau and especially Pavel Mintyukov the keys to the blue line will help in the long run, but it might make an already porous group even more vulnerable in front of goalie Lukas Dostal.

Add in a bottom-six forward group that doesn't match the depth of other conference contenders, and GM Pat Verbeek has some work to do before the Ducks can actualize as championship-caliber club. Of course, given the ages and contract status of their best core players, they're on that path even after a stumble this season.

Calgary Flames
Matvei Gridin becomes "must-watch"

As the Flames are mired in a rebuild, there aren't as many compelling reasons to make time for their games as there are for other Western Conference teams. Maybe watching Simon Nemec with a change in scenery? Possibly watching Dustin Wolf try to recapture the magic of his rookie season?

But if you're looking for a reason to tune in to a Calgary game, perhaps Matvei Gridin is that reason. The 20-year-old winger, drafted 28th overall in 2024, burst onto the scene with six goals and 14 assists in 37 games with the Flames, having popped for 10 goals in 37 games for their AHL affiliate. He's got decent size and some fun offensive tricks up his sleeve.

On a team that doesn't have a plethora of offensive stars, he has the potential to be one, giving hockey fans a reason to keep an eye on the Flames beyond their lottery odds.

Edmonton Oilers
Mike Babcock makes no statistical difference for McDavid, Draisaitl

It's still astonishing that Mike Babcock was given another head coaching job in the NHL, given what happened in Columbus and what we've come to learn about his time in Toronto and Detroit. But never underestimate the desire to win in this league, both from management and star players who buy into a coach's overstated legacy.

Connor McDavid and Leon Draisaitl both lobbied for Babcock's hiring. Draisaitl said, "We're looking to be coached. We're looking to get better. Connor and I sometimes deserve [criticism] too, just like anyone else does."

I'm still a bit hazy on the whole "Edmonton would have won the Stanley Cup by now if someone could just get a little more out of McDavid and Draisaitl" line of thought. I'm quite skeptical that his taskmaster will do anything to make them more effective than they already are. So the prediction here is that McDavid (4.4 points per 60 minutes) and Draisaitl (4.2) don't do better than their averages last season under Kris Knoblauch, who coached the Oilers to two Stanley Cup Finals but apparently didn't coach Connor and Leon.

Los Angeles Kings
Miss the playoffs

Peter Laviolette is governed by the law of diminishing returns. The Kings are his seventh NHL coaching gig. In his first full season coaching the Islanders, Hurricanes, Flyers, Predators, Capitals and Rangers, those teams all made the playoff cut. Four of them earned over 100 points in the standings in those seasons. Laviolette isn't shaking the "retread" label as the new coach in Los Angeles, but his track record is better than most.

Picking against a Laviolette team to make the playoffs is, in fact, a bold prediction. Since 2010, his teams only missed the playoffs three times when he's been behind the bench for the whole season. But as I keep looking at this offensively challenged team -- which was 29th in goals per game last season and subtracted Anze Kopitar -- I keep wondering how many goals Lavy can squeeze from a roster that might be a one-line team. (Albeit one line with Artemi Panarin, Quentin Byfield and Adrian Kempe on it.)

The relative weakness of the Pacific Division makes me a little concerned the Kings can eke out a sixth straight playoff berth. But why go through those motions for another first-round exit? Take the lottery ticket instead.

San Jose Sharks
Make the playoffs

The new Battle of California is over the third seed in the Pacific Division. Assuming the Oilers and Golden Knights remain the two best teams in the division -- and the Kraken, Flames and Canucks remain closer to the basement -- that leaves the Ducks, Kings and Sharks to vie for that last divisional playoff berth.

I think the Sharks earn it; or, failing that, one of the wild-card spots. In the process, playoff hockey comes back to the Shark Tank for the first time since 2019.

It all starts with Macklin Celebrini, whose 115-point season (!) willed the Sharks to a 34-point improvement in the standings from his rookie season. He has an incredibly young, talented group around him (Will Smith, Ivar Stenberg, Michael Misa), but one that suffers defensively as young groups do.

So GM Mike Grier added Darnell Nurse, Jacob Trouba and Michael Kesselring to improve the back end in the offseason, and veteran forward Mason Marchment to a group that already includes hard-working Kiefer Sherwood and Alexander Wennberg. They'll need Yaroslav Askarov to cover up some of their defensive deficiencies in goal this season in ways he couldn't last season. Admittedly, that's asking a lot, but hopefully an improved team in front of him makes a difference.

But who are we kidding: It's Celebrini or bust. He dragged a worse version of this team to within four points of the last wild-card spot in 2025-26, finishing fourth in the MVP race in the process. He started earning Sidney Crosby comparisons en masse last season. Please recall that Crosby had the Penguins playing for the Stanley Cup in Year 3. No pressure, Mack.

Seattle Kraken
Win the draft lottery

There might not be another franchise in the NHL right now that needs first overall pick more than the Kraken. It's not as if they're an abject disaster. They're just stuck in a hockey purgatory between contention and the basement. Worse yet, they're a team without a discernible draw. What comes to mind when I say "Seattle Kraken?" Exactly.

A first overall pick changes that. It's a shot of adrenaline to the heart. Look at what Matthew Schaefer did for the moribund Islanders. Granted, not everyone has his blessing of charisma, but every first overall pick is blessed with something else: Hope. That feeling of forward momentum that comes when your team lands the a potential future star in the lottery.

And hey, like Schaefer, the prize of next year's draft is also a dynamic young defenseman in Landon DuPont of Michigan. And he even played his junior hockey in Everett, to boot.

Vancouver Canucks
Marco Rossi becomes a No. 1 center

Rossi was acquired from the Wild in the Quinn Hughes trade last season. He spent parts of five seasons in Minnesota, which drafted him No. 9 in 2020. The expectation was that he could become the No. 1 center that they so desperately needed over the past few seasons. He didn't meet those expectations in the eyes of GM Bill Guerin, so off he went to Vancouver in exchange for their star defenseman.

Can he become that guy in Vancouver? The Canucks certainly hope so, either with them or to maximize his trade value ahead of needing a contract extension in 2029. Rossi showed flashes of that potential last season while playing with Brock Boeser, Vancouver's most accomplished scoring winger, especially when forward Liam Ohgren joined them to make an effective trio.

Here's how I would define "No. 1 center" in terms of this prediction: Rossi leads all Vancouver centers in ice time and points, and his lines are used in the most key situations for coach Manny Malhotra. I think he gets there. If not, then maybe Guerin was right.

Vegas Golden Knights
Mitch Marner scores 100 points

The Golden Knights have seen their share of accomplishments in the franchise's nine seasons. (Aw, they grow up so fast, don't they?) But there's one jackpot no Vegas player has yet to claim: Scoring 100 points in a season.

Jack Eichel has come the closest. He tallied 94 points in 77 games in 2024-25 and 90 points in 74 games last season. The common thread there: Not playing a full 82 games. If he did, Eichel would likely pass the century mark. But he's played more than 80 games just once in his career, as a Buffalo Sabres rookie in 2015-16.

Mitch Marner has played over 80 games in three of the past four seasons. He has also scored 100 points in a season, notching 102 in his walk year with the Maple Leafs in 2024-25. Last season, he had 80 points in 81 games for Vegas, which is a heck of an accomplishment given how much upheaval there was in his world that offseason.

While many projections have him topping out around 90 points, I think Marner has another 100-pointer in him. One thing to watch is on the power play, where he had 24 points (five goals, 19 assists) and can improve on those numbers. If he does, he could be the first Vegas player to roll 100 in the regular season.

stories.headline: Jones takes responsibility for Steveson leaving Octagon early
stories.summary: Jon Jones took responsibility for Gable Steveson's quick exit after a historic upset on Saturday, saying his instant reaction was to "get my friend to the back to make sure he was OK."
stories.body:
Gable Steveson, one of the biggest prospects in MMA history, has received a lot of criticism for immediately leaving the Octagon following his first professional loss Saturday in Los Angeles.

On Monday, Steveson's mentor and UFC legend Jon Jones took responsibility for Steveson's quick exit.

"I've seen some reports online and I really wanted to clear the air," Jones wrote on X. "It was my decision to take Gable straight to the back after the fight. Honestly it was the first time in this situation for me and my instant reaction was to get my friend to the back to make sure he was OK. Gable's work ethic and will to win is there and I stand by him and believe he will go on to be one of the best heavyweights in the UFC.

"He will be back I'm sure of it."

UFC commentator Daniel Cormier was among Steveson's critics after he left the Octagon, saying, "You cannot be a great winner but then an ungrateful loser, and I think that was bad by Steveson."

Sean Sharaf, who authored the monumental upset Saturday, said he wasn't greatly bothered by Steveson leaving early. Sharaf also told ESPN he expects the UFC to eventually book a rematch, given the history that was made in their first meeting.

"I know [the UFC] is going to want it," Sharaf said. "I already know the storyline, how it plays out, but I don't know. I think he's got to go do some reflecting and figure his stuff out because you can't underestimate anyone in this game no matter what. It's fighting and anything's possible."

An Olympic wrestling gold medalist and two-time NCAA Division I national champion, Steveson (4-1) suffered one of the biggest upsets in UFC history -- and in shocking fashion. Sharaf (4-2), who was 0-2 in the organization going into UFC 331 at Crypto.com Arena, knocked out Steveson with a left hook just 12 seconds into their main card matchup. It was the third-fastest knockout in UFC heavyweight history.

stories.headline: AFL player movement tracker: trade requests, free agency latest, who's on the move?
stories.summary: The offseason is upon us which means AFL trades, free agency, and player movement is about to take off. Here's the latest news, whispers, and confirmed deals.
stories.body:
It's AFL player movement season, with trades and free agency set to dominate the month of October. So who is going where? Keep track with our player movement guide here.

When is the AFL trade and free agency window?
The 2026 AFL trade period commences on Monday, October 5 and closes in the evening of Wednesday, October 14.

The free agency window opens and closes a little ealier; it runs from Friday, October 2 until Friday, October 9.

Tuesday, Sept. 22
Amartey officially names Carlton

Wantaway Sydney forward Joel Amartey has confirmed his desire to join Carlton as an unrestricted free agent.

The 26-year-old was kept out of the Swans' side with an Achilles injury in the latter stages of the year.

With Charlie Curnow (75 goals in 2026) and Logan McDonald (51) cementing their spots in the Sydney forward line as the prime targets, Amartey is hoping for more opportunity at the Blues.

Thursday, Sept. 17
GWS captain finally makes big call on his future

Toby Greene has opted to leave GWS, telling the AFL club he wishes to play with Geelong next season. Greene, who has been at the Giants since their foundation season in 2012, wants to go back to Victoria for family reasons.

In an extraordinary way to announce the decision, outgoing GWS boss Dave Matthews confirmed Greene's intentions on radio, before the club released a statement.

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join the Cats.

Saturday, Sept. 12
Zak Butters makes huge free agency call
The year's hottest restricted free agent Zak Butters has made a huge call on his future, nominating the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination.

After a year of speculation, with Geelong thought to be the front-runner for the Power star's signature, Butters made the call on Saturday, first reported by AFL.com.au's Callum Twomey.

The deal is reportedly for nine years.

Thursday, Sept. 10
Hogan set to join Pies
GWS and Collingwood have both confirmed that 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan has chosen the Magpies at his next home.

Set to be a four-club player, Hogan is 31 and coming off a 12-goal season from just nine appearances.

It's a big boost for the Magpies if Hogan can recapture his form; key forward has been an area of concern for a number of years.

Tuesday, Sept. 8
Bailey set to be Lion for life
Brisbane's Zac Bailey has ended months of 'will he, won't he' speculation to sign with the Lions for eight years, taking him through the 2034 season, the the club confirmed on Tuesday.

Bailey, a free agent, had been a big target for the Crows, who had reportedly tabled a more lucrative offer.

"I'm absolutely rapt to be staying at the Brisbane Lions," Bailey said in a statement.

"I love the environment here, the players, coaches and staff who all make it a great place to be and I feel like this Club continues to bring the best out of me.

"This Club means so much to me - I came here as a young player and have grown up here and to know I will be here long-term is something I'm really proud of.

"I would like to thank the club, my partner Em, my family and my management for being so supportive throughout this process.

"I love what we as a club have achieved during my time here and I am super excited about what we can continue to achieve together."

Rowan Marshall requests trade
St Kilda ruck Rowan Marshall looks set to be on the move, with the Saints confirming the big man had requested a trade for the second straight season.

While Marshall hasn't requested a specific club, it's likely to be Geelong after he failed to secure a trade to the Cats last year. He played 21 games for the Saints this seaosn, juggling ruck duties with Tom De Koning, who came in from Carlton last offseason.

"Rowan is a highly valued member of the St Kilda Football Club and remains contracted until the end of 2027," the Saints said in a statement.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club."

Zane Duursma wants to go to Melbourne
The No. 4 pick in the 2023 AFL draft Zane Duursma has requested a trade out of North Melbourne, with Melbourne in his sights.

The news comes a week after coach Alastair Clarkson was sacked by the club. North won nine games in 2026, their best return since 2019.

Ed Allan re-signs with the Pies
After speculation about his future at the Magpies, mdifielder Ed Allan has put pen to paper, signing a four year extension to remain at Collingwood.

2026 was a breakout season for Allan, who played 19 games and averaged a career-high 16.5 disposals per game.

Monday, Sept. 7
Pair of in-demand Dogs re-sign
According to afl.com.au, both Arty Jones and Buku Khamis will remain at the Kennel this offseason.

Jones will sign a three-year deal, while Khamis has a five-year contract in front of him.

Essendon and Brisbane had interest in livewire forward Jones, who had a standout performance against Collingwood in the wildcard final win, while the Blues were heavily linked to Khamis for a second straight offseason.

Cooper Hodge nomintes Hawthorn
A big boost for the Hawks, with club champion Luke Hodge's son Cooper choosing to join the Melbourne-based team as a father-son at this year's draft.

He had the option of going to Brisbane as a Lions academy member.

stories.headline: Isack Hadjar returns to Red Bull for Azerbaijan GP after injury layoff
stories.summary: Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar will return to action at this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the last three races with a wrist injury.
stories.body:
Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar will return to action at this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the last three races with a wrist injury.

The French driver injured his wrist while training during Formula 1's August break and was ruled out of the Dutch, Italian and Spanish Grands Prix as a result.

Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson substituted for Hadjar at all three races, while reserve driver Yuki Tsunoda took Lawson's place at the junior Red Bull team.

Hadjar's return at Red Bull means Lawson will now resume his season at Racing Bulls, with Tsunoda continuing on the sidelines as a potential stand-in for the rest of the season.

"Oracle Red Bull Racing is delighted to welcome Isack back this weekend," a Red Bull statement said. "Having made a successful recovery from his wrist injury, Isack will return to action at the Baku City Circuit on Thursday.

- Why is the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on a Saturday, not a Sunday?

- I raced against Max Verstappen... for 10 seconds: Inside the chaos of Max vs 100

"The team would like to sincerely thank Liam for his professionalism, dedication and hard work over the past three races. Stepping in under challenging circumstances, he delivered some impressive performances and made a valuable contribution to the team. We wish him all the very best as he returns to Visa Cash App Racing Bulls."

Lawson scored 14 points across the three rounds he was driving alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull, bringing his total points tally to 59 for the season.

While sitting out of the last three rounds, Hadjar had his one and only podium of the season reinstated by the FIA's International Court of Appeal after it overruled Alpine's right of review over the result of the Monaco Grand Prix earlier in the season.

stories.headline: Dreyer outduels Messi as San Diego hands Miami 4th straight draw
stories.summary: Lionel Messi scored his 101st goal for Inter Miami CF, but Anders Dreyer scored twice for San Diego FC, as the teams played to a 2-2 draw on Sunday night.
stories.body:
MIAMI -- Lionel Messi scored his 101st goal for Inter Miami CF, but Anders Dreyer scored twice for San Diego FC, as the teams played to a 2-2 draw on Sunday night.

It was Inter Miami's fourth consecutive draw in MLS play as new manager Kily González oversaw his first league game in charge of the club and cut a frustrated figure after conceding a late goal to drop points.

"We've been here for four days and haven't been able to train properly. Defensively, we really need to be much stronger," González said after the game. "We can't commit these defensive horrors, they come at a high cost. That final situation shouldn't have happened. It's surreal to be in a position to win the game, yet nearly lose it.

"We only avoided defeat because our goalkeeper saved us."

Dreyer gave San Diego a 1-0 lead in the 12th minute, capitalizing on a through ball from Jeppe Tverskov before deftly chipping over goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair.

Messi answered in the 24th with his 20th league goal of the season. His free kick from the right side went untouched through the penalty area and into the far side of the net, four days after he scored his 100th goal for Inter Miami in a 2-0 win over Mexican side Cruz Azul in the Campeones Cup.

"I think the Campeones Cup might have had an unconscious effect, especially in the first half, leading to a bit of complacency," González added. "These are factors that are part of football. At a club where we are obliged to win every match we play, we have to rise to the occasion. We made significant adjustments at halftime to get the team flowing and ensure we stayed compact, keeping the lines tight so we wouldn't suffer the way we did in the first half."

The goal was Messi's eighth from a free kick since entering the league in 2023, more than any other player in MLS during that time span.

Luis Suárez put Miami ahead in the 74th minute as Miami looked set to leapfrog New England into second place in the Eastern Conference, but Dreyer scored his second of the night eight minutes later with another fine finish -- this time from a ball over the top of the Herons' backline.

Miami is now in third place with a record of 12-4-10 with 46 points -- 11 behind first-place Nashville.

"But anyway, we have to keep going," González said. "On the positive side, we did some good things, but I need to fine-tune the defensive side because that's what really worries me most."

Earlier Sunday, FIFA announced that the final phase of the 2027 FIFA Women's Champions Cup will be played at Inter Miami's home of Nu Stadium in January. FIFA Chief Football Officer Jill Ellis spoke at halftime about bringing the competition to Miami.

"I think we've seen that this city loves its football. We've seen it this past summer with the World Cup," Ellis said. "I think it's time to bring a major women's tournament here to Miami. I think it's exciting."

Miami returns to MLS play next Sunday on the road against the Columbus Crew, while San Diego is also on the road with a game against Austin FC on Saturday.

ESPN writer Lizzy Becherano contributed to this report, while information from The Associated Press was also used.

stories.headline: Borussia Dortmund teenager Konstantinos Karetsas returns to training after Champions League health scare
stories.summary: Borussia Dortmund says 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.
stories.body:
Borussia Dortmund have said 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.

Karetsas passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass during Dortmund's 3-2 win over Villarreal on Sept. 8.

He was in tears as he was stretchered off with suspected circulatory problems and was then taken to a hospital, where he stayed for much of last week.

"Konstantinos Karetsas is back in team training as of Wednesday after doing individual sessions at the start of the week," Dortmund said. "It was his first joint session with his teammates after he was taken off with circulatory problems in the game against Villarreal."

Dortmund hasn't specified the nature of any diagnosis for Karetsas, who was signed from Genk for a reported fee of $34.6 million last month, and didn't indicate whether he would be able to play Saturday against Stuttgart in the Bundesliga.

Karetsas plays internationally for Greece but was born in Belgium, where local media have reported that dehydration was suspected as a factor.

"I'm doing really well," he said in a video recorded during a visit to his old club Genk and published Monday on X. "We tested everything and everything is fine. I just need to adjust a bit to the intensity but that will come with time."

"I went out with him but in that moment, he wasn't able to speak," Book said.

- Borussia Dortmund teenager Karetsas hospitalised after slumping to turf in Champions League

Karetsas was able to cheer on his teammates from the stands in Saturday's 3-0 win over Paderborn.

Managing director Lars Ricken said there had been "no warning signs" of any circulatory problems prior to the incident.

stories.headline: NRL Midweek Mail preliminary finals: Yeo and Leota keen to stay Panthers
stories.summary: Isaah Yeo and Moses Leota are both keens to remain Panthers despite interest elsewhere, while Casey McLean is happy for his departing brother.
stories.body:
The NRL rarely stands still.

Between training sessions, media appearances, and behind-the-scenes conversations, new storylines often begin to emerge before the weekend arrives.

Throughout the week, ESPN will be gathering notes, insights, and updates from around the competition heading into the NRL's preliminary finals weekend.

Yeo and Leota's future

Isaah Yeo has confirmed his preference is to remain at Penrith beyond his current contract, and is hoping to sort out his future following the end of the season.

"It always has been [my preference to stay]," Yeo admitted.

"The idea is to stay at Penrith as a one club player."

Moses Leota has also affirmed his love for Penrith, with the hope a deal gets done following the 2026 finals.

"[Remaining at Penrith] is massive to me," he shared.

"I've been here basically my whole life."

Casey McLean backs brother at Bulldogs

Panthers gun Casey McLean admitted while he's "gutted" that his brother Jesse will be leaving Penrith next year, but he's excited to see him flourish at Canterbury.

"Obviously pretty gutted that we won't be on the same team," he told ESPN.

"It'll be a weird feeling at first, but I'm super excited for the opportunity that he'll be given [at the Bulldogs]."

He went on to vouch for Jesse's ability on the field, expecting his older brother to remind fans of his talent.

"He does talk a little s--- on the field," Casey joked.

"But he's just an amazing player - he helped me grow as well.

"He's such an amazing role model, not only for myself, but for a fair few boys here as well."
